lines.caption: Every sentence of modern Japanese weaves together three different writing systems.
To see why, we have to go back to a time before Japan had writing at all.
For centuries, the language of these islands lived only in speech: in conversation, in song, and in memory.
Through centuries of contact with China and the Korean kingdoms, Chinese characters reached Japan, carried by scribes, scholars and Buddhist scriptures.
These characters, kanji, were created for Chinese, a very different language.
So scribes in Japan adapted them. Some kanji were used for their meaning. Others were borrowed purely for their sound.
Written quickly with a brush, those sound characters became softer and more flowing.
Over generations, the cursive forms were simplified into a new script: hiragana.
The kanji 安 (an), in flowing cursive, gradually became あ (a).
Buddhist monks and scholars, annotating Chinese texts, needed a quicker shorthand, so they often wrote just one part of a kanji.
The left side of 伊 (i) became the katakana イ (i).
Today, all three work together. Kanji carry meaning. Hiragana handle grammar. And katakana mostly write words borrowed from other languages.
私は日本語を勉強します。 I study Japanese.
Kanji give us "I", "Japanese" and "study". Hiragana supply the particles wa and o, and the verb shimasu.
From temple manuscripts to the screen in your hand, these scripts still carry Japanese culture and identity.
Nihongo. One language, three scripts, and centuries of history in every stroke.
